text: Next came a young man and a young woman called Trissie, both in the prime of youth, and he remarked that it was lucky it was not Friday, since they made you pay sixpence on Fridays. <break time="0.8s" /> When she asked what sixpence mattered anyway and whether it was not worth sixpence, he asked what she meant by it, and she could only answer, Oh, anything, I mean, you know what I mean. <break time="0.8s" /> After a pause, the couple stood still on the edge of the flower bed and together pressed the end of her parasol deep into the soft earth, his hand resting on the top of hers. <break time="0.8s" /> Their short, insignificant words were like short wings for a heavy body of meaning, too weak to carry it far and thus alighting awkwardly upon the very common objects around them. <break time="0.8s" /> When he said that it was time they had their tea, she asked with the oddest thrill of excitement where one had ones tea, remembering orchids, a Chinese pagoda, and a crimson crested bird, but he bore her on. <break time="0.8s" /> Thus one couple after another passed the flower bed with much the same irregular and aimless movement, and they were enveloped in layer after layer of green blue vapor, in which their bodies and colors slowly dissolved. <break time="0.8s" /> Voices, yes, wordless voices, broke the silence suddenly with deep contentment, passionate desire, or, in the voices of children, fresh surprise, but in truth there was no silence at all. <break time="0.8s" /> All the time the motor buses were turning their wheels, and the city murmured like a vast nest of Chinese boxes of steel, above which voices cried aloud and myriads of flowers flashed their colors into the air.
